::: {#thm-handshake}
#### The handshake theorem

For every graph $G = (V, E)$ (@def-graph-vertices-edges),

$$
\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2 \card{E},
$$

where $\deg(v)$ is the degree (@def-degree) of $v$ and $\card{E}$ is the number of edges (@def-cardinality).
It is called the handshake theorem [@wikipedia_handshaking_lemma]
because, when the vertices are the people at a party and the edges are the handshakes between them,
it says that the numbers of hands that the people shook add up to twice the number of handshakes.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

Each edge has two ends.
An edge with two endpoints has one end at each endpoint, and a loop has both ends at its one endpoint.
We count the set of all ends of all edges in two ways.

Counted edge by edge, each edge gives two ends, so there are $2 \card{E}$ ends.

Counted vertex by vertex, the ends at $v$ are one end of each non-loop edge with endpoint $v$
and two ends of each loop at $v$.
That is $\deg(v)$ ends, by @def-degree,
and each end is at exactly one vertex, so there are $\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v)$ ends.

The two counts count the same set, so they are equal.

:::

:::
